title: Cache Stampede
subtitle: Mitigating dogpiling and thundering herds using Singleflight Request Coalescing, Distributed Leases, and Probabilistic Early Expiration (XFetch).
keyTakeaways: A Cache Stampede occurs when a high-traffic key expires, triggering an instantaneous flood of concurrent cache misses that hammer the database with identical heavy queries.
In-process request coalescing (`Singleflight`) collapses duplicate misses on the same application pod into a single shared database query.
Probabilistic early expiration (such as the XFetch algorithm) and Soft TTLs trigger asynchronous background refreshes before keys hard-expire, preserving sub-millisecond read latencies.

sections.heading: Request Coalescing (Singleflight) and Distributed Mutex Leases
sections.body: When an expensive cached payload expires, every concurrent incoming thread sees a cache miss. Under high QPS, thousands of identical, redundant queries queue up at the database within fractions of a second, causing connection pool exhaustion and database CPU saturation. Resolving this requires deduplicating in-flight work.
bullets: In-Process Request Coalescing (`Singleflight`): Maintain a local concurrency map of `inflightPromises: Map<string, Promise<T>>`. If thread 1 is already querying the database for key X, threads 2 through 100 simply attach to the existing Promise. Across 20 application pods, database load drops from 1,000 queries to at most 20.

Distributed Mutex Leases (`SET lock:key 1 NX PX 2000`): To reduce those 20 pod queries down to exactly 1, the first pod to miss acquires a short-lived Redis lock. The winning pod computes the new value and updates Redis; the other 19 pods either wait briefly or immediately serve the slightly stale payload.
Never Hang on Locks: Enforce strict lock timeouts (e.g. 500ms) and always fall back to serving stale cached data or an empty payload rather than blocking client request threads indefinitely.

codeSnippet.title: In-Process Singleflight + Probabilistic Early Expiration (XFetch)

sections.heading: Probabilistic Early Refresh (XFetch Algorithm)
sections.body: Waiting for a hot key to hard-expire before coordinating a lock is inherently reactive. The XFetch algorithm (VLDB 2015) flips this by probabilistically refreshing hot data before expiration based on how long it takes to recompute.
bullets: How XFetch Works: Along with the cached value, store the computation time (`delta`). On every read hit, evaluate `now - delta * beta * ln(rand()) >= expiry`. If the random check passes, the reader triggers a background refresh.

Self-Scaling by Request Volume: Cold keys read once an hour almost never trigger early. A hot key receiving 2,000 reads per second will reliably trigger a quiet background refresh a few seconds before the TTL elapses, ensuring the key never experiences an open-window expiration.

Soft TTL with Background Async Worker: A simpler operational alternative is storing `soft_expire_at` in the JSON body. When the soft TTL passes, the first reader fires an async queue job to refresh Redis while immediately returning the current data to the user.

tradeOffs.pros: Strictly caps database load to 1 query cluster-wide even during cold starts or cache flushes.
tradeOffs.cons: Waiting callers on a cold key experience latency equal to the slowest database query duration.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Heavy analytical queries, reports, and cold-start application boot phases.

tradeOffs.pros: Zero latency penalty for end users because updates run asynchronously before hard expiration.
tradeOffs.cons: Requires items to already be cached; does not protect against misses on brand-new cold keys.
tradeOffs.bestFor: High-traffic homepages, public product detail endpoints, and low-latency API SLAs.

interviewTip: Pair both patterns: propose Soft TTL / Probabilistic Early Refresh to keep hot keys warm before expiration, and back it with Singleflight request coalescing to protect against cold-start misses.
